section.title: Indefinite Integrals and the Net Change Theorem

content.paragraph: We saw in Section 5.3 that the second part of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus provides a very powerful method for evaluating the definite integral of a function, assuming that we can find an antiderivative of the function. In this section we introduce a notation for antiderivatives, review the formulas for antiderivatives, and use them to evaluate definite integrals. We also reformulate FTC2 in a way that makes it easier to apply to science and engineering problems.

subsection.title: Indefinite Integrals
subsection.paragraph: Both parts of the Fundamental Theorem establish connections between antiderivatives and definite integrals. Part 1 says that if $$f$$ is continuous, then $$\int_{a}^{x}f(t)\mathit{dt}$$ is an antiderivative of $$f$$ . Part 2 says that $$\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\mathit{dx}$$ can be found by evaluating $$F(b) - F(a)$$ , where $$F$$ is an antiderivative of $$f$$ .

We need a convenient notation for antiderivatives that makes them easy to work with. Because of the relation between antiderivatives and integrals given by the Fundamental Theorem, the notation $$\int{f(x)\mathit{dx}}$$ is traditionally used for an antiderivative of $$f$$ and is called an indefinite integral. Thus
So we can regard an indefinite integral as representing an entire family of functions (one antiderivative for each value of the constant $$C$$ ).

You should distinguish carefully between definite and indefinite integrals. A definite integral $$\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\mathit{dx}$$ is a number , whereas an indefinite integral $$\int{f(x)\mathit{dx}}$$ is a function (or family of functions). The connection between them is given by Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem: if $$f$$ is continuous on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then

The effectiveness of the Fundamental Theorem depends on having a supply of antiderivatives of functions. We therefore restate the Table of Antidifferentiation Formulas from Section 4.9, together with a few others, in the notation of indefinite integrals. subsection.paragraph: Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem says that if $$f$$ is continuous on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , then
where $$F$$ is any antiderivative of $$f$$ . This means that $$F^{\prime} = f$$ , so the equation can be rewritten as

We know that $$F^{\prime}(x)$$ represents the rate of change of $$y = F(x)$$ with respect to $$x$$ and $$F(b) - F(a)$$ is the change in $$y$$ when $$x$$ changes from $$a$$ to $$b$$ . [Note that $$y$$ could, for instance, increase, then decrease, then increase again. Although $$y$$ might change in both directions, $$F(b) - F(a)$$ represents the net change in $$y$$ .] So we can reformulate FTC2 in words as follows.

subsection.paragraph: The principle expressed in the Net Change Theorem applies to all of the rates of change in the natural and social sciences that we discussed in Section 3.7. These applications show that part of the power of mathematics is in its abstractness. A single abstract idea (in this case the integral) can have many different interpretations. Here are a few instances of how the Net Change Theorem can be applied.

item.paragraph: If $$V(t)$$ is the volume of water in a reservoir at time $$t$$ , then its derivative $$V^{\prime}(t)$$ is the rate at which water flows into the reservoir at time $$t$$ . So
is the change in the amount of water in the reservoir between time $$t_{1}$$ and time $$t_{2}$$ .
If $$\lbrack C\rbrack(t)$$ is the concentration of the product of a chemical reaction at time $$t$$ , then the rate of reaction is the derivative $$d\lbrack C\rbrack \slash \mathit{dt}$$ . So
is the change in the concentration of $$C$$ from time $$t_{1}$$ to time $$t_{2}$$ .
If the mass of a rod measured from the left end to a point $$x$$ is $$m(x)$$ , then the linear density is $$\rho(x) = m^{\prime}(x)$$ . So
is the mass of the segment of the rod that lies between $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ .
If the rate of growth of a population is $$\mathit{dn} \slash \mathit{dt}$$ , then

is the net change in population during the time period from $$t_{1}$$ to $$t_{2}$$ . (The population increases when births happen and decreases when deaths occur. The net change takes into account both births and deaths.)
If $$C(x)$$ is the cost of producing $$x$$ units of a commodity, then the marginal cost is the derivative $$C^{\prime}(x)$$ . So
is the increase in cost when production is increased from $$x_{1}$$ units to $$x_{2}$$ units.
If an object moves along a straight line with position function $$s(t)$$ , then its velocity is $$\upsilon(t) = s^{\prime}(t)$$ , so

is the net change of position, or displacement, of the object during the time period from $$t_{1}$$ to $$t_{2}$$ . In Section 5.1 we guessed that this was true for the case where the object moves in the positive direction, but now we have proved that it is always true.

If we want to calculate the distance the object travels during the time interval, we have to consider the intervals when $$\upsilon(t) \geqslant 0$$ (the object moves to the right) and also the intervals when $$\upsilon(t) \leqslant 0$$ (the particle moves to the left). In both cases the distance is computed by integrating $$\left| {\upsilon(t)} \right|$$ , the speed. Therefore

note.title: A Note on Units
note.paragraph: How did we know what units to use for energy in Example 7? The integral $$\int_{0}^{24}{P(t)\mathit{dt}}$$ is defined as the limit of sums of terms of the form $$P\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)\Delta t$$ . Now $$P\left( t_{i}^{\ast} \right)$$ is measured in megawatts and $$\Delta t$$ is measured in hours, so their product is measured in megawatt-hours. The same is true of the limit. In general, the unit of measurement for $$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)\mathit{dx}}$$ is the product of the unit for $$f(x)$$ and the unit for $$x$$ .

subsection.title: Writing Project Newton, Leibniz, and the Invention of Calculus
subsection.paragraph: We sometimes read that the inventors of calculus were Sir Isaac Newton (1642–1727) and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716). But we know that the basic ideas behind integration were investigated 2500 years ago by ancient Greeks such as Eudoxus and Archimedes, and methods for finding tangents were pioneered by Pierre Fermat (1601–1665), Isaac Barrow (1630–1677), and others. Barrow––who taught at Cambridge and was a major influence on Newton––was the first to understand the inverse relationship between differentiation and integration. What Newton and Leibniz did was to use this relationship, in the form of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, in order to develop calculus into a systematic mathematical discipline. It is in this sense that both Newton and Leibniz are credited with the invention of calculus.
